screens.title: Compound Indexes and Index Properties
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how compound indexes let MongoDB optimize queries that touch more than one field. We will explain the practical rule for ordering fields — Equality, then Sort, then Range — and show how that order changes whether an index is used efficiently. You will also learn about covered queries, where MongoDB returns results from the index alone without reading documents, and why that can be dramatically faster. Finally, we cover index properties you will use in real systems: partial indexes for indexing only a subset of documents, TTL indexes to expire old data, and unique indexes to enforce data integrity. For example, an online store that searches by category and sorts by price benefits from a compound index on category and price; a covered query can avoid disk fetches if both the query fields and the projected fields are in the index. By the end of this lesson you will be able to pick index orders that follow ESR, design covered queries when possible, and choose partial, TTL, or unique indexes based on use case. Consider: what query pattern in your application is currently slow and might be fixed by a compound index?

screens.title: What is a Compound Index?
screens.narratorSegment: A compound index is an index that includes multiple fields in a defined order so MongoDB can traverse entries in that combined order. In practice, compound indexes optimize queries that filter on several fields or filter on one field and sort on another. To make this concrete, think of a phone book arranged first by last name and then by first name. If you look for "Smith, John" the phone book points directly to a small block of entries. If you look for first name only, you lose most of the ordering. Similarly, an index defined as { lastName: 1, firstName: 1 } supports queries that filter by lastName and then by firstName, and it supports queries that filter by lastName alone. It will not efficiently support queries that filter only by firstName. An important behavior to remember is that the index order is directional: the leftmost fields are the most selective for using the index. A common misconception is that a compound index will accelerate all permutations of those fields; it will not. The correct mental model is: the index provides an ordered path starting at the leftmost field and continues rightward. Practice by listing the common query filters in your application and order index fields so those filters map to left-to-right traversal.

keyIdea.title: Core definition
keyIdea.text: A compound index orders entries across multiple fields. The left-to-right order determines which query shapes can use the index efficiently.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › What is a Compound Index?
Analogy: Phone book
A phone book sorted by last name then first name lets you find all entries for a last name quickly and then quickly scan first names within that block.
Definition
A compound index contains multiple fields in a specific order. MongoDB walks the index from left to right and can efficiently support queries that match a prefix of those fields.
Example
{ lastName: 1, firstName: 1 }
Supports queries on lastName, and on lastName plus firstName, but not firstName alone.
Key Takeaway
Index order matters. Match it to how your application filters and sorts data.
Common misconception
A compound index does not accelerate queries that only use non-leftmost fields. People often expect it to act like multiple single-field indexes; it does not.
Concrete scenario
E-commerce
Index:{ category: 1, price: -1 } helps queries that filter by category and sort by price descending, returning already-sorted results from the index traversal.
Key Takeaway

Design compound indexes to match frequently used query prefixes; leftmost fields are the most important.

screens.title: The ESR Rule: Equality, Sort, Range
screens.narratorSegment: The ESR rule is a practical ordering guideline: put Equality fields first, then Sort fields, then Range fields. Equality fields are exact-match predicates, such as userId or category. Sort fields are those you use in an explicit sort operation to order results, like transactionDate when sorting by recency. Range fields are those used with greater-than or less-than comparisons, such as price greater than a threshold. Placing equality fields first narrows the search quickly, then placing sort fields allows the index to produce results in the desired order without an in-memory sort, and placing range fields last ensures range scans are applied after the index prefix is matched. An important constraint to remember is that a compound index can effectively use only one range predicate; if multiple fields use range operators, only the leftmost range is fully used. A concrete example: if you frequently query transactions by userId, then sort by transactionDate descending, then filter by amount range, the index order should be { userId: 1, transactionDate: -1, amount: 1 }. Use this sequence as you map real query patterns: list equality filters, then sort keys, then any range filters, and order index fields accordingly.

keyIdea.title: ESR ordering
keyIdea.text: Place fields in the order: Equality, then Sort, then Range. This maximizes the chance the index is used for filtering and sorting.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › ESR Rule
ESR — Stepwise index ordering
Follow these steps to map your query to an index ordering that MongoDB can use efficiently.
01 Equality
Fields used with exact matches. These narrow the result set most effectively and should come first.
Example: userId, category
02 Sort
Fields you sort on so the index can return results already ordered and avoid an in-memory sort.
Example: transactionDate, price
03 Range
Range predicates come last. Only the leftmost range predicate is fully used in a compound index scan.
Example: amount > 100, price < 1000
Concrete index
{ userId: 1, transactionDate: -1, amount: 1 }
Equality on userId, sort on transactionDate, range on amount.
Common pitfall
Placing a range-field left of a sort-field can prevent the index from satisfying the sort, causing an extra sort step.
Key Takeaway

List equality filters first, then sort keys, then range filters. Use this mapping to choose index order before creating an index.

screens.title: Why Field Order Changes Query Efficiency
screens.narratorSegment: Field order in a compound index controls which query shapes are efficiently supported. Consider two indexes: { a: 1, b: 1 } and { b: 1, a: 1 }. The first supports queries that filter on a, or on a and b, with good performance. It will not support queries that filter only on b efficiently. Conversely, the second supports queries on b and on b and a. This means you should align index field order with the most common query prefixes in your application. For example, if most queries filter by category and then sort by price, use { category: 1, price: -1 }. If you instead create { price: -1, category: 1 } your queries filtering by category would not benefit. Another important point: a compound index supports index-only prefixes. If you need both a and b frequently together, include them in that order. A common misconception is expecting one compound index to replace multiple single-field indexes for all query permutations. It does not. Choose indexes by examining actual query logs or profiling and by testing with explain to confirm which index is used. What query prefix shows up most in your app logs?

keyIdea.title: Order affects coverage
keyIdea.text: Choose the left-to-right order based on common query prefixes; an index is most useful for queries matching its leftmost fields.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Field Order Comparison
Index A: { a: 1, b: 1 }
Supports queries that filter on a, or on a and b together. Efficient for a-first query patterns.
Good query
find({ a: 5, b: 10 }) — index prefix matched, fast IXSCAN possible.
Poor query
find({ b: 10 }) — index not efficient for b-only lookups when a is not in predicate.
Index B: { b: 1, a: 1 }
Supports queries that filter on b, or on b and a together. It flips which single-field queries are efficient.
Good query
find({ b: 10, a: 5 }) — prefix matched on b then a.
Poor query
find({ a: 5 }) — may not be able to use the compound index effectively.
Practical check

Inspect your query logs and profile output. Create candidate indexes that match the most frequent query prefixes and verify with explain that IXSCAN is used.

screens.title: Covered Queries: Return from the Index Only
screens.narratorSegment: A covered query is one where every field used in the query predicate and every field returned in the projection are present in the same index. When that happens, MongoDB can satisfy the query using only the index and skip fetching documents from the collection. This reduces disk access and is typically much faster. For example, with an index on category and price you can write a query that filters on category and projects price; both fields exist in the index, so MongoDB can read the index entries and return price without fetching the full document. One nuance is the _id field: it is included in indexes by default, so requests that include _id can still be covered; if you explicitly exclude _id in projection, it is not required from the index. A common mistake is projecting fields not present in the index, which breaks coverage and forces document fetches. The safe practice is to design narrow projections for index-covered queries and verify coverage by checking explain output that indicates no document fetch or shows an index-only plan. Try this on your dataset with small projections first.

keyIdea.title: Covered query advantage
keyIdea.text: If predicate and projection fields are all in an index, MongoDB can return results from the index alone, avoiding document fetches.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Covered Queries
Example index and covered query
Create an index that contains both the filtered field and the projected field.
db.products.createIndex({ category: 1, price: -1 })

// Covered query:
db.products.find(
  { category: "Electronics" },
  { price: 1, _id: 0 }
).explain("executionStats")
If category (predicate) and price (projection) are both in the index, MongoDB can return price directly from the index entries.
Mistake to avoid
Projecting a field not in the index forces a document fetch and breaks coverage.
Quick checklist
  • Does the index include every filter field?
  • Does the index include every projected field?
  • Is _id projected or excluded explicitly?
Key Takeaway

Design projections to match index fields to enable index-only answers and avoid costly document fetches.

screens.title: Partial Indexes: Index a Subset of Documents
screens.narratorSegment: Partial indexes let you create an index that only contains documents matching a filter expression. This is useful when a subset of documents is queried frequently while the rest are rarely used. For example, if your users collection has many inactive accounts but queries mostly target active users, you can create an index that only includes documents where status is active. This reduces index size and write maintenance, and can improve cache behavior for queries that target that subset. The syntax uses partialFilterExpression to define the predicate for which documents to index. A common use case is high-value items in a product catalog: index only products above a price threshold. A trap to avoid is assuming the partial index will be used for queries that don't include the filter condition; for best results, include the partial index predicate in your query so MongoDB can match the index entries. Always verify with explain whether the partial index is selected for the query you expect it to accelerate. Partial Indexes: Index a Subset of Documents means partial indexes reduce index size by indexing only documents that match a filter, improving performance for targeted query subsets.. In practical terms, when to index only matching documents and how it helps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Partial Indexes
Create a partial index
Example: index only active users to keep index small and focused.
db.users.createIndex(
  { status: 1 },
  { partialFilterExpression: { status: "active" } }
)
Only documents where status equals "active" are included in the index.
When to use
When a predictable subset of documents is queried frequently and the remainder rarely needs indexing.
Check
Run explain on the target query and verify the partial index is selected. Ensure the query includes the partial filter condition for best results.
Key Takeaway

Use partial indexes to shrink index size and speed queries for a specific subset, but remember the query must match the filter for index selection.

screens.title: TTL Indexes: Automatic Expiration
screens.narratorSegment: TTL indexes remove documents automatically after a specified amount of time. Create a single-field index on a date field and set expireAfterSeconds to the number of seconds after which documents become eligible for deletion. This is ideal for session stores, caches, and short-lived log entries. For example, creating a TTL index on a createdAt field with expireAfterSeconds equal to 3600 will mark documents older than one hour for deletion. MongoDB periodically checks and removes expired documents in the background. Note that TTL uses the date value in the indexed field to determine age; if the field is missing or not a date, TTL behavior will differ. A practical tip is to ensure your application sets the date field correctly at write time. Also, TTL indexes are single-field only; you cannot make a compound TTL index. When designing data retention, confirm the deletion schedule aligns with your retention policy and test on a staging cluster before production. TTL Indexes: Automatic Expiration means create a single-field index on a date and set expireafterseconds to automate removal of old documents, useful for sessions and caches.. In practical terms, set up automatic cleanup using a date field. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › TTL Indexes
Create a TTL index
Example: expire documents older than 3600 seconds using createdAt.
db.log_events.createIndex(
  { createdAt: 1 },
  { expireAfterSeconds: 3600 }
)
Documents with createdAt older than one hour will be removed by MongoDB's background task.
Notes
TTL indexes are single-field only. Ensure the date field is set correctly for each document and test deletion timing in a staging environment.
Use cases
  • Session documents
  • Temporary caches
  • Short-lived logs and events
Key Takeaway

Use TTL to automate deletion of time-bound data, but confirm the date field semantics and deletion schedule before production use.

screens.title: Unique Indexes: Enforcing Data Integrity
screens.narratorSegment: Unique indexes enforce that no two documents in a collection can have the same value for the indexed field or combination of fields. They are a fundamental mechanism for preserving data integrity in MongoDB. A common example is enforcing unique email addresses in a users collection by creating an index with { unique: true } on the email field. You can also create compound unique indexes to enforce uniqueness of a field combination, such as firstName and lastName together to prevent exact duplicates of a name combination. When a duplicate insertion is attempted after creating a unique index, MongoDB will return an error and the write will fail. A practical workflow is to ensure existing data conforms to uniqueness before creating the index — you can find duplicates using aggregation — and to add unique indexes as part of a controlled migration. Unique indexes also interact with partial indexes: a partial unique index can enforce uniqueness only for the indexed subset of documents. Use unique indexes to move validation logic from the application into the database where it is atomic and enforced consistently.

Create a unique index
Example: enforce unique productCode values across the products collection.

Attempting to insert a duplicate productCode after this index exists will return an error and the insert will fail.

screens.title: Testing Indexes with explain()
screens.narratorSegment: Testing and validating index behavior is an essential step after creation. The chapter provides hands-on steps you can follow: create the compound index for your query pattern — for example creating an index on category and price — then run explain with executionStats to see whether MongoDB uses the index. You should look for winningPlan. stage indicating IXSCAN and that totalKeysExamined is low relative to the collection size. If your query does an equality on the leftmost fields and a sort matching index order, expect an IXSCAN and avoid an in-memory sort. Try the reverse scenario where the query uses the range or sort fields in the wrong order: explain often shows a COLLSCAN or a higher keys-examined count. The chapter also walks through creating a unique productCode and attempting an insert that duplicates a value to observe the write error. For partial indexes, run explain on a query that matches the partialFilterExpression to confirm the partial index is chosen, and test a query that does not match to confirm the partial index is not used. These explain checks are your verification loop before deploying indexes to production.

keyIdea.title: Verify with explain
keyIdea.text: Use explain('executionStats') to confirm IXSCAN usage, low keys examined, and that covered or partial indexes are selected when expected.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Testing with explain()
Create and test a compound index
Follow the pattern to create the index, then run explain to inspect the plan.
use cohortia_shop;
db.products.createIndex({ category: 1, price: -1 });

// Test ideal ESR match
db.products.find({ category: "Category 10" }).sort({ price: -1 }).explain("executionStats");

// Test ESR mismatch case
db.products.find({ price: { $gt: 500 } }).sort({ category: 1 }).explain("executionStats");
Check that winningPlan.stage is IXSCAN and totalKeysExamined is low for the ideal case. For the mismatch case, explain may show COLLSCAN or higher keys examined.
Interpretation checklist
  • Is IXSCAN present in winningPlan?
  • Are totalKeysExamined low relative to collection size?
  • Is an in-memory sort being avoided?
Key Takeaway

Always verify index effectiveness with explain before relying on it in production; adjust index order or fields when explain shows inefficient plans.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Design Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: When designing indexes, watch for several frequent mistakes. First, misordering fields against the ESR rule can cause MongoDB to skip using the index effectively or to perform in-memory sorts. Second, attempting to use multiple range predicates in a compound index expects only the leftmost range to be used; if your query uses ranges on multiple fields, consider alternate index strategies or application-side filtering. Third, expecting a compound index to accelerate all permutations of the fields is incorrect — queries must match a left-prefixed subset of the index fields. Fourth, creating broad indexes for every possible query leads to high write overhead; prefer targeted indexes guided by actual query patterns and profiling. Good design patterns include: index the equality fields you use most often at the left, add sort fields next when those sorts are frequent, use partial indexes when a small subset needs indexing, and use unique indexes to enforce invariants. Always test candidate indexes with explain and monitor keys examined and whether MongoDB uses IXSCAN for expected queries. Finally, document your indexes and the query patterns they serve so future maintenance is easier.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Design Patterns & Pitfalls
Common mistakes
  • Placing fields in an order that conflicts with query patterns, breaking ESR.
  • Expecting multiple range predicates to be equally usable; only the leftmost range is prioritized.
  • Relying on one compound index for all permutations of queries; it won't cover all shapes.
  • Creating broad or unnecessary indexes without verifying query benefit, increasing write cost.
Pattern: Targeted indexes
Use partial indexes and narrow compound indexes that match frequent query prefixes to limit maintenance cost and maximize benefit.
Pattern: Verify with explain
Measure IXSCAN usage, keys examined, and whether an in-memory sort occurs. Iterate on index order based on these signals.
Learner prompt

Identify one slow query in your app and map its equality, sort, and range fields. Could a compound index following ESR improve it? Try creating a candidate index and verify with explain.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how compound indexes let MongoDB optimize queries that touch more than one field. We will explain the practical rule for ordering fields — Equality, then Sort, then Range — and show how that order changes whether an index is used efficiently. You will also learn about covered queries, where MongoDB returns results from the index alone without reading documents, and why that can be dramatically faster. Finally, we cover index properties you will use in real systems: partial indexes for indexing only a subset of documents, TTL indexes to expire old data, and unique indexes to enforce data integrity. For example, an online store that searches by category and sorts by price benefits from a compound index on category and price; a covered query can avoid disk fetches if both the query fields and the projected fields are in the index. By the end of this lesson you will be able to pick index orders that follow ESR, design covered queries when possible, and choose partial, TTL, or unique indexes based on use case. Consider: what query pattern in your application is currently slow and might be fixed by a compound index?

These objectives map to practical skills you will use when designing indexes. First, you will design and implement compound indexes to support queries that combine fields. That includes choosing the right field order so the index is useful for both filtering and sorting. Second, you will apply the ESR rule — place equality predicates first, then any sort fields, then range predicates — and understand its limits, such as only one range predicate being effectively used. Third, you will learn to recognize and construct covered queries so MongoDB can return results directly from an index without fetching documents, which reduces disk access. Finally, you will create partial and TTL indexes when you need smaller, targeted indexes or automatic expiration, and implement unique indexes to enforce data integrity constraints. Each objective includes a short example or mnemonic so you can remember the rule and verify competency with an execution plan. As you progress, you'll connect these objectives to real tasks like speeding product searches and enforcing uniqueness for keys like email or product codes.

These continuation objectives focus on practical validation and constraints. You will practice creating compound indexes and using explain output to confirm the index is used; check for IXSCAN stages and that totalKeysExamined is low compared to the collection size. You will design partial indexes when only a subset of documents needs indexing — for example indexing only active users — which reduces maintenance overhead. You will set up TTL indexes on date fields to automatically remove expired documents, such as session entries or logs older than a threshold. Finally, you will implement unique indexes to prevent duplicate values for fields like email or a generated product code. Each objective includes a simple test you can run: create the index, run an explain plan, and validate that the index is chosen and that document fetches were avoided for covered queries. These steps prepare you to implement and verify indexes in a production dataset safely.

A compound index is an index that includes multiple fields in a defined order so MongoDB can traverse entries in that combined order. In practice, compound indexes optimize queries that filter on several fields or filter on one field and sort on another. To make this concrete, think of a phone book arranged first by last name and then by first name. If you look for "Smith, John" the phone book points directly to a small block of entries. If you look for first name only, you lose most of the ordering. Similarly, an index defined as { lastName: 1, firstName: 1 } supports queries that filter by lastName and then by firstName, and it supports queries that filter by lastName alone. It will not efficiently support queries that filter only by firstName. An important behavior to remember is that the index order is directional: the leftmost fields are the most selective for using the index. A common misconception is that a compound index will accelerate all permutations of those fields; it will not. The correct mental model is: the index provides an ordered path starting at the leftmost field and continues rightward. Practice by listing the common query filters in your application and order index fields so those filters map to left-to-right traversal.

The ESR rule is a practical ordering guideline: put Equality fields first, then Sort fields, then Range fields. Equality fields are exact-match predicates, such as userId or category. Sort fields are those you use in an explicit sort operation to order results, like transactionDate when sorting by recency. Range fields are those used with greater-than or less-than comparisons, such as price greater than a threshold. Placing equality fields first narrows the search quickly, then placing sort fields allows the index to produce results in the desired order without an in-memory sort, and placing range fields last ensures range scans are applied after the index prefix is matched. An important constraint to remember is that a compound index can effectively use only one range predicate; if multiple fields use range operators, only the leftmost range is fully used. A concrete example: if you frequently query transactions by userId, then sort by transactionDate descending, then filter by amount range, the index order should be { userId: 1, transactionDate: -1, amount: 1 }. Use this sequence as you map real query patterns: list equality filters, then sort keys, then any range filters, and order index fields accordingly.

Field order in a compound index controls which query shapes are efficiently supported. Consider two indexes: { a: 1, b: 1 } and { b: 1, a: 1 }. The first supports queries that filter on a, or on a and b, with good performance. It will not support queries that filter only on b efficiently. Conversely, the second supports queries on b and on b and a. This means you should align index field order with the most common query prefixes in your application. For example, if most queries filter by category and then sort by price, use { category: 1, price: -1 }. If you instead create { price: -1, category: 1 } your queries filtering by category would not benefit. Another important point: a compound index supports index-only prefixes. If you need both a and b frequently together, include them in that order. A common misconception is expecting one compound index to replace multiple single-field indexes for all query permutations. It does not. Choose indexes by examining actual query logs or profiling and by testing with explain to confirm which index is used. What query prefix shows up most in your app logs?

A covered query is one where every field used in the query predicate and every field returned in the projection are present in the same index. When that happens, MongoDB can satisfy the query using only the index and skip fetching documents from the collection. This reduces disk access and is typically much faster. For example, with an index on category and price you can write a query that filters on category and projects price; both fields exist in the index, so MongoDB can read the index entries and return price without fetching the full document. One nuance is the _id field: it is included in indexes by default, so requests that include _id can still be covered; if you explicitly exclude _id in projection, it is not required from the index. A common mistake is projecting fields not present in the index, which breaks coverage and forces document fetches. The safe practice is to design narrow projections for index-covered queries and verify coverage by checking explain output that indicates no document fetch or shows an index-only plan. Try this on your dataset with small projections first.

Partial indexes let you create an index that only contains documents matching a filter expression. This is useful when a subset of documents is queried frequently while the rest are rarely used. For example, if your users collection has many inactive accounts but queries mostly target active users, you can create an index that only includes documents where status is active. This reduces index size and write maintenance, and can improve cache behavior for queries that target that subset. The syntax uses partialFilterExpression to define the predicate for which documents to index. A common use case is high-value items in a product catalog: index only products above a price threshold. A trap to avoid is assuming the partial index will be used for queries that don't include the filter condition; for best results, include the partial index predicate in your query so MongoDB can match the index entries. Always verify with explain whether the partial index is selected for the query you expect it to accelerate. Partial Indexes: Index a Subset of Documents means partial indexes reduce index size by indexing only documents that match a filter, improving performance for targeted query subsets.. In practical terms, when to index only matching documents and how it helps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

TTL indexes remove documents automatically after a specified amount of time. Create a single-field index on a date field and set expireAfterSeconds to the number of seconds after which documents become eligible for deletion. This is ideal for session stores, caches, and short-lived log entries. For example, creating a TTL index on a createdAt field with expireAfterSeconds equal to 3600 will mark documents older than one hour for deletion. MongoDB periodically checks and removes expired documents in the background. Note that TTL uses the date value in the indexed field to determine age; if the field is missing or not a date, TTL behavior will differ. A practical tip is to ensure your application sets the date field correctly at write time. Also, TTL indexes are single-field only; you cannot make a compound TTL index. When designing data retention, confirm the deletion schedule aligns with your retention policy and test on a staging cluster before production. TTL Indexes: Automatic Expiration means create a single-field index on a date and set expireafterseconds to automate removal of old documents, useful for sessions and caches.. In practical terms, set up automatic cleanup using a date field. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Unique indexes enforce that no two documents in a collection can have the same value for the indexed field or combination of fields. They are a fundamental mechanism for preserving data integrity in MongoDB. A common example is enforcing unique email addresses in a users collection by creating an index with { unique: true } on the email field. You can also create compound unique indexes to enforce uniqueness of a field combination, such as firstName and lastName together to prevent exact duplicates of a name combination. When a duplicate insertion is attempted after creating a unique index, MongoDB will return an error and the write will fail. A practical workflow is to ensure existing data conforms to uniqueness before creating the index — you can find duplicates using aggregation — and to add unique indexes as part of a controlled migration. Unique indexes also interact with partial indexes: a partial unique index can enforce uniqueness only for the indexed subset of documents. Use unique indexes to move validation logic from the application into the database where it is atomic and enforced consistently.

Testing and validating index behavior is an essential step after creation. The chapter provides hands-on steps you can follow: create the compound index for your query pattern — for example creating an index on category and price — then run explain with executionStats to see whether MongoDB uses the index. You should look for winningPlan. stage indicating IXSCAN and that totalKeysExamined is low relative to the collection size. If your query does an equality on the leftmost fields and a sort matching index order, expect an IXSCAN and avoid an in-memory sort. Try the reverse scenario where the query uses the range or sort fields in the wrong order: explain often shows a COLLSCAN or a higher keys-examined count. The chapter also walks through creating a unique productCode and attempting an insert that duplicates a value to observe the write error. For partial indexes, run explain on a query that matches the partialFilterExpression to confirm the partial index is chosen, and test a query that does not match to confirm the partial index is not used. These explain checks are your verification loop before deploying indexes to production.
